claim: The Spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 is extensively glycosylated.
source: The Spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, its receptor-binding domain (RBD), and its primary receptor ACE2 are extensively glycosylated.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of the Spike protein.

claim: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is extensively glycosylated.
source: The Spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, its receptor-binding domain (RBD), and its primary receptor ACE2 are extensively glycosylated.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of the RBD.

claim: ACE2 is extensively glycosylated.
source: The Spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, its receptor-binding domain (RBD), and its primary receptor ACE2 are extensively glycosylated.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of ACE2.

claim: N- and O-glycans have only minor contribution to Spike-ACE2 binding.
source: We observed that N- and O-glycans had only minor contribution to Spike-ACE2 binding.
evidence: Experimental observation from binding studies reported in the abstract.

claim: N- and O-glycans play a major role in regulating viral entry.
source: However, these carbohydrates played a major role in regulating viral entry.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays reported in the abstract.

claim: Blocking N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage using genetic approaches dramatically reduced viral entry into ACE2 expressing HEK293T cells.
source: Blocking N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage using both genetic approaches and the small molecule kifunensine dramatically reduced viral entry into ACE2 expressing HEK293T cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout cells reported in the abstract.

claim: Blocking N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage using kifunensine dramatically reduced viral entry into ACE2 expressing HEK293T cells.
source: Blocking N-glycan biosynthesis at the oligomannose stage using both genetic approaches and the small molecule kifunensine dramatically reduced viral entry into ACE2 expressing HEK293T cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays using kifunensine treatment reported in the abstract.

claim: Blocking O-glycan elaboration partially blocked viral entry.
source: Blocking O-glycan elaboration also partially blocked viral entry.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays reported in the abstract.

claim: Inhibition of N-glycan biosynthesis enhanced Spike-protein proteolysis.
source: Among them, inhibition of N-glycan biosynthesis enhanced Spike-protein proteolysis.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Enhanced Spike-protein proteolysis can reduce RBD presentation on virus.
source: This could reduce RBD presentation on virus, lowering binding to host ACE2 and decreasing viral entry.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation of experimental data presented in the abstract.

claim: Reduced RBD presentation on virus lowers binding to host ACE2.
source: This could reduce RBD presentation on virus, lowering binding to host ACE2 and decreasing viral entry.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation of experimental data presented in the abstract.

claim: Reduced RBD presentation on virus decreases viral entry.
source: This could reduce RBD presentation on virus, lowering binding to host ACE2 and decreasing viral entry.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation of experimental data presented in the abstract.

claim: Chemical inhibitors of glycosylation may be evaluated for COVID-19.
source: Overall, chemical inhibitors of glycosylation may be evaluated for COVID-19.
evidence: Proposed therapeutic application based on experimental findings in the abstract.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus causing the global pandemic 'coronavirus diseases 2019' (COVID-19).
source: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus causing the global pandemic 'coronavirus diseases 2019' (COVID-19).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is a zoonotic beta-coronavirus from bats.
source: This is a zoonotic beta-coronavirus from bats that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 causes severe acute respiratory syndrome.
source: This is a zoonotic beta-coronavirus from bats that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 unleashes a cytokine storm to alter immune response.
source: Its effects on human physiology extends well beyond the lung as it unleashes a cytokine storm to alter immune response (Chen et al., 2020) and cause disseminated intravascular coagulation (Lillicrap, 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 causes disseminated intravascular coagulation.
source: Its effects on human physiology extends well beyond the lung as it unleashes a cytokine storm to alter immune response (Chen et al., 2020) and cause disseminated intravascular coagulation (Lillicrap, 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Lillicrap, 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 exhibits multiorgan tropism that impacts kidney, liver, heart and brain function.
source: It also exhibits multiorgan tropism that impacts kidney, liver, heart and brain function (Puelles et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Puelles et al., 2020.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is critical for viral attachment, fusion and entry into host.
source: Among its structural elements, the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein is critical for viral attachment, fusion and entry into host (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2003; Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2003; Lan et al., 2020.

claim: The RBD region of Spike enables binding to its primary human cellular receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2).
source: The RBD region of Spike enables binding to its primary human cellular receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2), which is ubiquitously expressed on epithelial, endothelial and blood cells (Li et al., 2003; Hamming et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Li et al., 2003; Hamming et al., 2004.

claim: ACE2 is ubiquitously expressed on epithelial, endothelial and blood cells.
source: The RBD region of Spike enables binding to its primary human cellular receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 (ACE2), which is ubiquitously expressed on epithelial, endothelial and blood cells (Li et al., 2003; Hamming et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Li et al., 2003; Hamming et al., 2004.

claim: A role for heparan sulfates in viral entry has been proposed.
source: A role for heparan sulfates in viral entry has also been proposed (Clausen et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed mechanism cited in the introduction with reference to Clausen et al., 2020.

claim: Viral fusion and entry depends on the furin/RRAR-S site located between the Spike S1 and S2 subunits.
source: Once bound, viral fusion and entry depends on two proteolysis sites, the furin/RRAR-S site located between the Spike S1 and S2 subunits, and a second S2'/SKR-S site (Belouzard et al., 2009).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Belouzard et al., 2009.

claim: Viral fusion and entry depends on the S2'/SKR-S site.
source: Once bound, viral fusion and entry depends on two proteolysis sites, the furin/RRAR-S site located between the Spike S1 and S2 subunits, and a second S2'/SKR-S site (Belouzard et al., 2009).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with reference to Belouzard et al., 2009.

claim: TMPRSS2 (transmembrane protease, serine 2) may aid viral entry.
source: A variety of enzymes including TMPRSS2 (transmembrane protease, serine 2) and cathepsin-L may aid viral entry (Hoffmann et al., 2020b; Matsuyama et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Hoffmann et al., 2020b; Matsuyama et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2020.

claim: Cathepsin-L may aid viral entry.
source: A variety of enzymes including TMPRSS2 (transmembrane protease, serine 2) and cathepsin-L may aid viral entry (Hoffmann et al., 2020b; Matsuyama et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Hoffmann et al., 2020b; Matsuyama et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2020.

claim: The Spike protein has 22 N-glycosylation sites.
source: Both the viral Spike-protein and ACE2 receptor are extensively glycosylated, with a majority of the 22 N-glycosylation sites of Spike and 7 N-glycosylation sites of ACE2 bearing carbohydrates (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a; Figure 1).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a.

claim: ACE2 has 7 N-glycosylation sites.
source: Both the viral Spike-protein and ACE2 receptor are extensively glycosylated, with a majority of the 22 N-glycosylation sites of Spike and 7 N-glycosylation sites of ACE2 bearing carbohydrates (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a; Figure 1).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a.

claim: A majority of the 22 N-glycosylation sites of Spike bear carbohydrates.
source: Both the viral Spike-protein and ACE2 receptor are extensively glycosylated, with a majority of the 22 N-glycosylation sites of Spike and 7 N-glycosylation sites of ACE2 bearing carbohydrates (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a; Figure 1).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a.

claim: A majority of the 7 N-glycosylation sites of ACE2 bear carbohydrates.
source: Both the viral Spike-protein and ACE2 receptor are extensively glycosylated, with a majority of the 22 N-glycosylation sites of Spike and 7 N-glycosylation sites of ACE2 bearing carbohydrates (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a; Figure 1).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Shajahan et al., 2020a.

claim: The exact distribution of oligomannose, hybrid, complex, sialylated, and fucosylated structures in Spike and ACE2 is likely dictated both by the protein structure and host expression system.
source: The exact distribution of the oligomannose, hybrid, complex, sialylated, and fucosylated structures in these macromolecules is likely dictated both by the protein structure and host expression system (Shajahan et al., 2020b; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Shajahan et al., 2020b; Watanabe et al., 2020.

claim: O-linked glycans are reported on both Spike protein and ACE2.
source: O-linked glycans are also reported on both proteins (Shajahan et al., 2020a; Shajahan et al., 2020b).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction with references to Shajahan et al., 2020a; Shajahan et al., 2020b.

claim: Glycans have been proposed to function in immunological shielding.
source: A variety of functions have been proposed for these glycans including immunological shielding (Watanabe et al., 2020), direct regulation of Spike-ACE2 binding (Bernardi et al., 2020), and control of Spike up/down conformation (Casalino et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed function cited in the introduction with reference to Watanabe et al., 2020.

claim: Glycans have been proposed to directly regulate Spike-ACE2 binding.
source: A variety of functions have been proposed for these glycans including immunological shielding (Watanabe et al., 2020), direct regulation of Spike-ACE2 binding (Bernardi et al., 2020), and control of Spike up/down conformation (Casalino et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed function cited in the introduction with reference to Bernardi et al., 2020.

claim: Glycans have been proposed to control Spike up/down conformation.
source: A variety of functions have been proposed for these glycans including immunological shielding (Watanabe et al., 2020), direct regulation of Spike-ACE2 binding (Bernardi et al., 2020), and control of Spike up/down conformation (Casalino et al., 2020).
evidence: Proposed function cited in the introduction with reference to Casalino et al., 2020.

claim: Experimental data supporting the proposed functions of glycans is currently lacking.
source: Experimental data supporting these concepts is currently lacking and thus our understanding of the impact of glycosylation on SARS-CoV-2 function is incomplete.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Glycans cover the Spike-ACE2 interface.
source: Glycans cover the Spike-ACE2 interface.
evidence: Observation from molecular dynamics simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Glycans surround the putative proteolysis site of furin ('S1-S2').
source: They also surround the putative proteolysis site of furin ('S1-S2', yellow) and S2' (blue).
evidence: Observation from molecular dynamics simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Glycans surround the S2' proteolysis site.
source: They also surround the putative proteolysis site of furin ('S1-S2', yellow) and S2' (blue).
evidence: Observation from molecular dynamics simulation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RBD-Fc has an apparent molecular mass of ~60 kDa.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RBD-Fc has a theoretical mass of 51 kDa based on peptide alone.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Calculated theoretical mass based on peptide sequence.

claim: S1-Fc has an apparent molecular mass of ~150 kDa.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 2B.

claim: S1-Fc has a theoretical mass of 101 kDa based on peptide alone.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Calculated theoretical mass based on peptide sequence.

claim: ACE2-Fc has an apparent molecular mass of ~140 kDa.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ACE2-Fc has a theoretical mass of 110 kDa based on peptide alone.
source: Thus, RBD-Fc was ~60 kDa instead of a theoretical mass of 51 kDa, S1-Fc was ~150 kDa rather than 101 kDa, and ACE2-Fc was ~140 kDa instead of 110 kDa (Figure 2B).
evidence: Calculated theoretical mass based on peptide sequence.

claim: RBD-Fc and S1-Fc readily bound to HEK293T cells upon human ACE2 over-expression.
source: RBD-Fc and S1-Fc readily bound to HEK293T cells upon human ACE2 over-expression, confirming that they are functionally active (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ACE2-Fc specifically bound Spike-protein expressed on 293Ts.
source: ACE2-Fc also specifically bound Spike-protein expressed on 293Ts.
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Desialylation of Spike-protein expressed on 293 T/S had minimal effect on ACE2-Fc binding.
source: Desialylation of Spike-protein expressed on 293 T/S had minimal effect on ACE2-Fc (0.7 µg/mL) binding.
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ACE2 desialylation on 293T/ACE2 increased binding of RBD-Fc by 26%.
source: ACE2 desialylation on 293T/ACE2 increased binding of RBD-Fc (0.2 µg/mL) and S1-Fc (1.7 µg/mL) by 26–56% (paired experiments, *p<0.05).

claim: ACE2 desialylation on 293T/ACE2 increased binding of S1-Fc by 56%.
source: ACE2 desialylation on 293T/ACE2 increased binding of RBD-Fc (0.2 µg/mL) and S1-Fc (1.7 µg/mL) by 26–56% (paired experiments, *p<0.05).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: VSVG pseudotyped virus infected both HEK293T and stable 293T/ACE2 cells.
source: VSVG pseudotyped virus infected both HEK293T (black line) and stable 293T/ACE2 (red line) cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Virus with Spike-WT entered 293T/ACE2 only.
source: Virus with Spike-WT and Spike-mutant entered 293T/ACE2 only.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Virus with Spike-mutant entered 293T/ACE2 only.
source: Virus with Spike-WT and Spike-mutant entered 293T/ACE2 only.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Infection using Spike-mutant was higher compared to Spike-WT.
source: Infection using Spike-mutant was higher compared to Spike-WT.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Sialidase treatment of virus had no effect on viral entry.
source: Sialidase treatment of virus had no effect.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Sialidase treatment of 293T/ACE2 cells did not affect VSVG pseudovirus entry.
source: Sialidase treatment did not affect viral entry.

claim: Sialidase treatment of 293T/ACE2 cells did not affect Spike-WT pseudovirus entry.
source: Sialidase treatment did not affect viral entry.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ~80–100% of the N-glycans expressed at specific sites of ACE2-Fc were complex-type glycans.
source: In this regard, independent glycoprotemics mass spectrometry (MS) data showed that ~80–100% of the N-glycans expressed at specific sites of ACE2-Fc and ~40–100% of the S1-Fc glycopeptides expressed complex-type glycans (K.C., et al., manuscript in preparation).

claim: ~40–100% of the S1-Fc glycopeptides expressed complex-type glycans.
source: In this regard, independent glycoprotemics mass spectrometry (MS) data showed that ~80–100% of the N-glycans expressed at specific sites of ACE2-Fc and ~40–100% of the S1-Fc glycopeptides expressed complex-type glycans (K.C., et al., manuscript in preparation).
evidence: Glycoproteomics mass spectrometry data from unpublished manuscript.

claim: Up to ~60% of the antennae on complex structures on ACE2 were terminated by sialic acid.
source: Up to ~60% of the antennae on these complex structures on ACE2 and ~20% of the structures on S1-Fc were terminated by sialic acid.
evidence: Glycoproteomics mass spectrometry data from unpublished manuscript.

claim: Up to ~20% of the structures on S1-Fc were terminated by sialic acid.
source: Up to ~60% of the antennae on these complex structures on ACE2 and ~20% of the structures on S1-Fc were terminated by sialic acid.

claim: Sanger sequencing confirmed that all three C1GalT1 alleles of [O]-293T contained indels.
source: Sanger sequencing confirmed that all three C1GalT1 alleles of [O]-293T contained indels (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Frameshift mutation was noted at the single MGAT1 allele in [N]-293T.
source: Frameshift mutation was also noted at the single MGAT1 allele in [N]-293T.
evidence: Experimental observation from Sanger sequencing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: VVA-lectin binding to GalNAcα was dramatically augmented in the [O]-293Ts.
source: As anticipated, VVA-lectin (Vicia villosa agglutinin) binding to GalNAcα was dramatically augmented in the [O]-293Ts (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry lectin binding assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Complex glycans were absent in [N]-293Ts as they did not engage PHA-L.
source: Complex glycans were absent in [N]-293Ts as they did not engage PHA-L (lectin from Phaseolus vulgaris).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry lectin binding assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Knocking out N-glycans on Spike protein reduced ACE2-Fc binding by 40%.
source: Here, we observed a 40% decrease in ACE2-Fc binding to cell-surface Spike expressed on [N]-293Ts, and a slight 20% increase when Spike was expressed on the [O]-293Ts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knocking out O-glycans on Spike protein increased ACE2-Fc binding by 20%.
source: Here, we observed a 40% decrease in ACE2-Fc binding to cell-surface Spike expressed on [N]-293Ts, and a slight 20% increase when Spike was expressed on the [O]-293Ts (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Glycan engineering of ACE2 in the [O]- and [N]-293Ts did not impact S1-Fc binding.
source: Glycan engineering of ACE2 in the [O]- and [N]-293Ts did not impact either S1-Fc (Figure 3E) or RBD-Fc binding (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Glycan engineering of ACE2 in the [O]- and [N]-293Ts did not impact RBD-Fc binding.
source: Glycan engineering of ACE2 in the [O]- and [N]-293Ts did not impact either S1-Fc (Figure 3E) or RBD-Fc binding (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RBD-Fc bound ~10 times more avidly to ACE2 compared to S1-Fc.
source: Here, RBD-Fc bound ~10 times more avidly to ACE2 compared to S1-Fc.
evidence: Experimental observation from flow cytometry binding assay comparing Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence.
source: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT and Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence (Figure 4B), and a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence.
source: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT and Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence (Figure 4B), and a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT pseudovirus resulted in a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells.
source: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT and Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence (Figure 4B), and a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells.
source: When produced in [O]-293T, Spike-WT and Spike-mutant pseudovirus resulted in a 70–85% loss in DsRed fluorescence (Figure 4B), and a partial reduction (35–70%) in the fraction of DsRed positive cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knocking out N-glycans in both Spike-WT and Spike-mutant pseudoviruses abrogated viral infection into 293T/ACE2 cells by >95%.
source: In stark contrast, knocking out N-glycans in both pseudoviruses abrogated viral infection into 293T/ACE2 cells by >95% (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Both the Spike-WT and Spike-mutant virus expressed comparable levels of Spike protein, regardless of the glycosylation mutation.
source: Western blot with anti-S2 pAb (polyclonal antibody) suggest that both the Spike-WT and Spike-mutant virus expressed comparable levels of Spike protein, regardless of the glycosylation mutation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The molecular mass of Spike expressed in [N]-293T was lower than that of other virus consistent with the extensive N-glycosylation of this protein.
source: The molecular mass of Spike expressed in [N]-293T was lower than that of other virus consistent with the extensive N-glycosylation of this protein.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Spike-WT is more extensively cleaved compared to Spike-mutant.
source: Additionally, the data suggest more extensive cleavage of Spike-WT compared to Spike-mutant, consistent with the presence of the proteolysis-sensitive polybasic furin-site in Spike-WT.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 4E.

claim: N-glycan loss may trigger precipitous (95%, based on densitometry) loss of intact Spike protein due to enhanced cleavage at the S1-S2 interface.
source: This blot suggests that N-glycan loss may trigger precipitous (95%, based on densitometry) loss of intact Spike protein due to enhanced cleavage at the S1-S2 interface.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 4F with densitometry analysis.

claim: Virus produced in [O]-293Ts showed greater proteolysis (52%) compared to that produced in wild-type 293Ts (32%).
source: Consistent with the viral entry assay, we also noted greater proteolysis of virus produced in [O]-293Ts (52%) compared to that produced in wild-type 293Ts (32%).
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 4F with densitometry analysis.

claim: Kifunensine reduced the formation of complex N-glycans on cultured cells within 24–48 hr with no change in cell viability.
source: This water-soluble inhibitor reduced the formation of complex N-glycans on cultured cells within 24–48 hr with no change in cell viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental observation from lectin binding and viability assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Virus produced in culture with 15 µM kifunensine displayed ~85–90% reduction in infection.
source: Virus produced in culture with 15 µM kifunensine displayed ~85–90% reduction in infection, as measured using DsRed-reporter in microscopy (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and cytometry assays (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 5B, 5C, 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduction in Spike molecular mass upon addition of kifunensine was less apparent compared to that in [N]-293Ts.
source: The reduction in Spike molecular mass upon addition of this small molecule was less apparent compared to that in [N]-293Ts (Figure 5E), since blockade of Mannosidase-I preferentially gives rise to Man7-9 glycans while the MGAT1/[N]-293Ts knockouts produce Man-5.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 5E with mechanistic explanation.

claim: Blockade of Mannosidase-I preferentially gives rise to Man7-9 glycans.
source: The reduction in Spike molecular mass upon addition of this small molecule was less apparent compared to that in [N]-293Ts (Figure 5E), since blockade of Mannosidase-I preferentially gives rise to Man7-9 glycans while the MGAT1/[N]-293Ts knockouts produce Man-5.
evidence: Established knowledge about the mechanism of kifunensine action.

claim: MGAT1/[N]-293Ts knockouts produce Man-5 glycans.
source: The reduction in Spike molecular mass upon addition of this small molecule was less apparent compared to that in [N]-293Ts (Figure 5E), since blockade of Mannosidase-I preferentially gives rise to Man7-9 glycans while the MGAT1/[N]-293Ts knockouts produce Man-5.
evidence: Established knowledge about the glycan structure produced by MGAT1 knockout.

claim: Spike-protein proteolysis was more extensive upon kifunensine addition though it was not complete.
source: Here also, the Spike-protein proteolysis was more extensive upon kifunensine addition though it was not complete, as observed in the anti-FLAG blot.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kifunensine reduced DsRed expression in 293T/ACE2 cells, even in the case of Spike-delta pseudovirus.
source: In viral entry assay, kifunensine reduced DsRed expression in 293T/ACE2 cells, even in the case of Spike-delta pseudovirus (*p<0.05).
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 5F with statistical analysis.

claim: The substitution of the 'RRAR' sequence with a single Alanine ('A') resulted in viral Spike that was not extensively cleaved both in the absence and presence of kifunensine.
source: The substitution of the 'RRAR' sequence with a single Alanine ('A') resulted in viral Spike that was not extensively cleaved both in the absence and presence of kifunensine.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Robust viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells was observed using furin resistant virus (Spike-delta).
source: Robust viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells was observed using this furin resistant virus, and this too could be partially blocked by kifunensine.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Viral entry of furin resistant virus (Spike-delta) could be partially blocked by kifunensine.
source: Robust viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells was observed using this furin resistant virus, and this too could be partially blocked by kifunensine.
evidence: Experimental observation from pseudovirus entry assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: N-glycans may have additional roles during viral entry beyond regulating proteolysis at the S1-S2 site.
source: Thus, in addition to proteolysis at the S1-S2 site, N-glycans may have additional roles during viral entry.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation that kifunensine reduces entry of Spike-delta virus.

claim: Some enhancement in Spike binding and viral entry was observed upon treating 293T/ACE2 with a pan-sialidase.
source: In this regard, we observed some enhancement in Spike binding and viral entry upon treating 293T/ACE2 with a pan-sialidase.
evidence: Experimental observation from binding and viral entry assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The critical glycans regulating Spike-ACE2 binding are likely located at Asn-90 or Asn-322, proximal to the Spike binding interface.
source: Based on the published crystal structure and molecular modeling, the critical glycans regulating this process are likely located at Asn-90 or Asn-322, proximal to the Spike binding interface (Lan et al., 2020; Figure 1).
evidence: Inference based on published crystal structure and molecular modeling with reference to Lan et al., 2020.

claim: The effect of sialic acid on SARS-CoV-2 was small compared to that reported for other sialic acid dependent viruses like influenza.
source: The effect was nevertheless small compared to that reported for other sialic acid dependent viruses like influenza (Stencel-Baerenwald et al., 2014), reovirus, parovirus (Löfling et al., 2013) and coronavirus like the Middle-East Respiratory Syndrome virus/MERS (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with published literature on other viruses with references to Stencel-Baerenwald et al., 2014; Löfling et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017.

claim: Blocking O- and N-glycan biosynthesis on ACE2 did not impact either viral entry or Spike-Fc binding.
source: Here, blocking O- and N-glycan biosynthesis on ACE2 did not impact either viral entry or Spike-Fc binding.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry and binding assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The functional change observed upon enzymatically removing sialic acid on ACE2 is likely a steric effect, as it can be offset by other modifications.
source: Thus, the functional change observed upon enzymatically removing sialic acid on ACE2 is likely a steric effect, as it can be offset by other modifications.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data comparing sialidase treatment with glycan knockout effects.

claim: Blocking elaboration of O- and N-glycans on Spike only had a partial effect on ACE2-Fc binding.
source: Blocking elaboration of O- and N-glycans on Spike, also, only had a partial effect on ACE2-Fc binding.
evidence: Experimental observation from binding assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The active/'up' form of Spike RBD is largely exposed with few glycans at the binding interface.
source: This observation is consistent with previous cryo-EM (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020) and molecular dynamics simulation results (Grant et al., 2020), which show that the active/'up' form of Spike RBD is largely exposed with few glycans at the binding interface.
evidence: Established knowledge from published cryo-EM and molecular dynamics studies with references to Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Grant et al., 2020.

claim: The lack of glycan shielding makes the exposed RBD a prime target for vaccine development.
source: It is now well appreciated that this lack of glycan shielding, makes the exposed RBD a prime target for vaccine development.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field about vaccine development strategies.

claim: Blocking N-glycan elaboration using genetic approaches dramatically reduced viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
source: In this regard, we observed that blocking N-glycan elaboration using both genetic approaches (i.e. MGAT1-KO/[N]-293T) and the natural product mannosidase-I inhibitor, kifunensine, dramatically reduced viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Blocking N-glycan elaboration using kifunensine dramatically reduced viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
source: In this regard, we observed that blocking N-glycan elaboration using both genetic approaches (i.e. MGAT1-KO/[N]-293T) and the natural product mannosidase-I inhibitor, kifunensine, dramatically reduced viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from viral entry assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: Enzymatic and small molecule inhibition resulted in enhanced proteolysis of Spike-protein during pseudovirus production.
source: In the case of Spike-mut, enzymatic and small molecule inhibition resulted in enhanced proteolysis of Spike-protein during pseudovirus production.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot analysis discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: There is an inverse relation between furin cleavage and viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
source: These data suggest an inverse relation between furin cleavage and viral entry into 293T/ACE2 cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations comparing Spike-WT and Spike-mut viral entry.

claim: Spike-mut displayed reduced S1-S2 proteolysis compared to Spike-WT, and higher viral infectivity.
source: Consistent with this, Spike-mut displayed reduced S1-S2 proteolysis compared to Spike-WT, and higher viral infectivity.
evidence: Experimental observation from western blot and viral entry assays discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The introduction of the D614G mutation in Spike reduced furin cleavage, and this resulted in enhanced viral infectivity.
source: Finally, a recent study observed that the introduction of the D614G mutation in Spike reduced furin cleavage, and this resulted in enhanced viral infectivity (Korber et al., 2020).
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Korber et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 containing the D614G mutation is currently the dominant strain worldwide (>80% prevalence).
source: SARS-CoV-2 containing the D614G mutation is currently the dominant strain worldwide (>80% prevalence, Zhang et al., 2020), and the possibility that this is due to altered furin cleavage potential is hotly debated.
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Both N- and O-glycans may modulate the rates of proteolysis at the S1-S2 interface, thus affecting viral entry.
source: Overall, our studies with MGAT1-KO, C1GalT1-KO and kifunensine suggest that both N- and O-glycans may modulate the rates of proteolysis at the S1-S2 interface, thus affecting viral entry (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inference from experimental observations with glycan knockout cells and kifunensine treatment.

claim: Some S1 may be associated with Spike even after partial cleavage at the S1-S2 interface.
source: While some S1 may be associated with Spike even after partial cleavage at the S1-S2 interface (Belouzard et al., 2009), this may potentiate a quantitative reduction in RBD presentation on viral surface, resulting in reduced ACE2 binding and lower viral entry.
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Belouzard et al., 2009.

claim: Partial cleavage at the S1-S2 interface may potentiate a quantitative reduction in RBD presentation on viral surface, resulting in reduced ACE2 binding and lower viral entry.
source: While some S1 may be associated with Spike even after partial cleavage at the S1-S2 interface (Belouzard et al., 2009), this may potentiate a quantitative reduction in RBD presentation on viral surface, resulting in reduced ACE2 binding and lower viral entry.
evidence: Mechanistic interpretation of experimental data.

claim: Several N-glycans are located proximal to the furin-site: N603 and N657, and also N61.
source: Indeed several N-glycans are located proximal to the furin-site: N603 and N657, and also N61 (Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Watanabe et al., 2020.

claim: O-glycans have been hypothesized to exist in the furin-site region at S673, T678 and S686.
source: O-glycans have also been hypothesized to exist in this region at S673, T678 and S686 (Andersen et al., 2020), and some of these have been experimentally verified (Sanda et al., 2020).
evidence: Published hypothesis and experimental verification cited with references to Andersen et al., 2020; Sanda et al., 2020.

claim: The effect of 'Spike-delta' mutation may be cell type specific in that this mutation results in lower infectivity in some cell types like Calu-3 which rely on the enzyme TMPRSS2 for viral fusion.
source: Others have noted that the effect of 'Spike-delta' mutation may be cell type specific in that this mutation results in lower infectivity in some cell types like Calu-3 which rely on the enzyme TMPRSS2 for viral fusion, while this mutation does not affect entry into other cell types like VeroE6 which lacks TMPRSS2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Hoffmann et al., 2020b.

claim: The 'Spike-delta' mutation does not affect entry into cell types like VeroE6 which lacks TMPRSS2.
source: Others have noted that the effect of 'Spike-delta' mutation may be cell type specific in that this mutation results in lower infectivity in some cell types like Calu-3 which rely on the enzyme TMPRSS2 for viral fusion, while this mutation does not affect entry into other cell types like VeroE6 which lacks TMPRSS2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Hoffmann et al., 2020b.

claim: Additional glycosylation sites proximal to S2' may also modulate viral entry, perhaps because some proteases like TMPRSS2 have both ligand-binding and protease activity.
source: Based on these observations, we speculate that additional glycosylation sites proximal to S2' may also modulate viral entry, perhaps because some proteases like TMPRSS2 have both ligand-binding and protease activity.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental observations and published literature.

claim: The N-glycans proximal to S2' include N801, and to a lesser extent N616 and N657.
source: The N-glycans proximal to S2' include N801, and to a lesser extent N616 and N657.
evidence: Structural information about glycan locations.

claim: Both O- and N-glycan truncation may be used to reduce viral entry.
source: In addition to basic science understanding, our findings have translational potential as it suggests that both O- and N-glycan truncation may be used to reduce viral entry.
evidence: Proposed therapeutic application based on experimental findings.

claim: It would be attractive to test additional N-glycosylation inhibitors, like Swainsonine, which has a demonstrated safety profile in humans.
source: In this regard, it would be attractive to test additional N-glycosylation inhibitors, like Swainsonine, which has a demonstrated safety profile in humans (Goss et al., 1997).
evidence: Proposed therapeutic approach with reference to Goss et al., 1997 for safety profile.

claim: Swainsonine has a demonstrated safety profile in humans.
source: In this regard, it would be attractive to test additional N-glycosylation inhibitors, like Swainsonine, which has a demonstrated safety profile in humans (Goss et al., 1997).
evidence: Published observation cited with reference to Goss et al., 1997.

claim: Glycoengineering may provide a strategy to take advantage of evolutionary features to regulate viral entry and reduce disease transmission.
source: Overall, while SARS-CoV-2 has developed a natural ability to enhance infectivity, we propose that glycoengineering may provide a strategy to take advantage of these evolutionary features to regulate viral entry and reduce disease transmission.
evidence: Proposed therapeutic strategy based on experimental findings.

claim: ~45–100% of the viral N-glycans were complex-type.
source: Glycoproteomics analysis of purified pseudovirus produced in HEK293T cells showed that ~45–100% of the viral N-glycans were complex-type, with up to ~55% of their antennae being terminated by sialic acid (K.C., et al. manuscript in preparation).
evidence: Glycoproteomics mass spectrometry data from unpublished manuscript.

claim: Up to ~55% of the antennae on viral N-glycans were terminated by sialic acid.
source: Glycoproteomics analysis of purified pseudovirus produced in HEK293T cells showed that ~45–100% of the viral N-glycans were complex-type, with up to ~55% of their antennae being terminated by sialic acid (K.C., et al. manuscript in preparation).
evidence: Glycoproteomics mass spectrometry data from unpublished manuscript.

claim: The pseudovirus used in this study was processed by glycoenzymes that are typically found in the cellular medial and trans-Golgi compartments.
source: Thus, the pseudovirus used in this study was processed by glycoenzymes that are typically found in the cellular medial and trans-Golgi compartments.
evidence: Inference from glycoproteomics data showing complex-type glycans.

claim: ACE2 sialic acids may modestly shield virus/Spike binding in some biological contexts and perhaps some cell systems.
source: Together, the binding and pseudovirus data suggest that ACE2 sialic acids may modestly shield virus/Spike binding in some biological contexts and perhaps some cell systems.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental data from binding and viral entry assays.
